utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina, et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber is aware that there is a scheduling issue. We'll deal with that later today, not at this very moment. Mr. Moric, good morning to you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you again that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Are you ready, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would appreciate if you try to finish in two sessions, certainly not more.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will try my best, Mr. President. Thank you. Mr. Registrar, may have I document D1759, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Prosecutor. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, we noted during direct examination that you issued an order to reopen the roads on 8 August, and this is at transcript reference 2556. In fact, Mr. Mikulicic brought that order up which showed the roads being opened on 22nd -- I'm sorry, on 8 August at 2200 hours. Now that was pursuant to the closure of the roads at 3.00 a.m. on 4 August. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Prosecutor, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think the document that's on -- it's D1759. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is the order by which you closed the roads; isn't that correct, Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have D1769 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then after opening the roads on 8 August, you also issued an order prohibiting access to the liberated areas. That is, restricting movements to unauthorised persons. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if I could have D1769 on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In fact, you can see the -- you order on the screen. It says arrival of reports and public figures in the liberated area. "Allow all reporters accredited in the Republic of Croatia to work freely without necessary permission [sic] in the area of Petrina and the Plitvice Lakes, but permission from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and Ministry of Interior is needed for other liberated areas."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "When distinguished and generally known public persons enter the liberated area, you must consult the duty operations of operative action staff, MUP Povratak staff, and for all other persons access to the liberated area is prohibited until further notice." So you, by this order, restricted access generally to all persons, unauthorised persons to the liberated area; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber as to how this order was implemented on the ground. Was it by means of the civilian police check-points? How was it implemented on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By means of the civilian police check-points, yes. There was no other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Now, moving on, Mr. Moric --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have document P203 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: During direct examination -- while that document is coming up, you will not be familiar with that document. My question to you is: During direct examination when Mr. Mikulicic showed you the 18th August order - that is, for the record, D49 - and it was discussed, you were asked as to when you got information on the increase in the number of crimes. And let me tell you exactly what you said. This is at transcript page 25561. Your answer was, you said: "If I rely on the date of this document, which is the 18th of August, then my assessment would be that that my co-workers and myself realise that we are facing a deluge of crimes and that pattern began a few days before that day, let's say around the 15th of August." Now, do you see on the screen, Mr. Moric, this is a report from Mr. Ante Gugic head of security information to the minister of defence and Dr. Miroslav Tudjman send on 8th August. In paragraph 4 the report reads: "In the liberated area ... of hinterlands of Zadar and Sibenik the establishment of the civilian authorities is not being carried out in a satisfactory pace. More precisely, in the liberated settlements" -- and there are settlements indicated there, including Djevrska and Kistanje, "the situation is rather chaotic. Incidents of mass burning of houses, plundering of property, alcohol consumption occur and the units lack organisation. The reason for such a situation is the insufficient engagement of the command personnel of the units." Now, were you informed of the situation on 8th August, or perhaps the following day, on 9th August, by any person, either by the minister of the interior or any other agency?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As for the villages indicated here, Bribirske Mostine, Djevrska, and Kistanje, I was not informed about them in such a way. Nobody informed me, either the minister or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, even apart from these villages, on or around 8th August, were you informed by either the minister of the interior or any agency, other agency, Ministry of Defence, or from other intelligence services that there was a problem about military personnel burning houses and committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody informed me about that. It was not logical to discuss a possible problem in the military with me, or inform me about that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, if the witness is permitted to read the whole document, that page and the next page, to put this matter in context, and I'm talking about that paragraph and the next paragraph, I think it would assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, if you prefer to read the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: However Mr. Kehoe, could always address if there are any issues in re-examination, Mr. President. But I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He could. Let's not argue the matter. Also if you can prevent in a neutral way to get half of the answers now and that the remainder of the answer later on, then it could have be preferable to have the right answer right away. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, if you prefer to read the entire document, and perhaps the next page also, and if you have any additional comment to make regarding this issue, please do so. Have you read the entire document?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the meantime, the document has been turned to the following page. Could we please go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you read this document? Do you have anything to add or comment on this matter? We just read it -- on the point that I have discussed with you.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there is another relevant piece of information in the last paragraph on page 1. In the last and penultimate lines, the author of this information says that he had informed the police administration of Zadar and Knin about the problems that had been noticed in the aforementioned villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, going back to my question earlier on, if you had been informed about the problem about military personnel burning houses and committing crimes, about -- on or about the 8th August, your answer was, Nobody informed me about that. It was not logical to discuss a possible problem in the military with me or inform me about that problem. So is it your position, Mr. Moric, that when to comes to crimes committed by military personnel, generally, you were not informed of that because you were in the Ministry of Interior. Is it -- is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my testimony. My testimony is in regard with the specific villages in this document. As for any problems that involved members of the Croatian Army or people in uniform sporting the visual identity of the Croatian Army is something that I was informed about in terms of that being a trend, a type of problem that prevailed or appeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber as to when, what were the first time after the liberation you heard about this trend of persons in military uniforms committing crimes? When -- when was the first time you heard, approximately? Now, earlier on, you said about the 15th of August. Now, I'm pointing out that this information was available to the Ministry of Defence on or around 8 August. Now, when did you hear about it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific about the time when I heard that. I can't give you the exact day, or date. This information is about three villages, three very specific villages, so I really can't tell you when it was that I heard about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, isn't it correct that you heard about military personnel committing crimes as early as 7th August?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Isn't it correct that, in fact, you telephoned Major-General Lausic and informed him about this problem on 7th August?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I don't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- then let's look at a document, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can I have, Mr. Registrar, P2174, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what I'm going show you, Mr. Moric, is an extract of Mr. Lausic's diary, which is in evidence in these proceedings. That's P2174. This, as you can see, is an entry for 7th August, and you note at -- Mr. Lausic has made an entry that at 1845 hours, assistant minister of the Ministry of Interior, J. Moric, has contacted him, and he says: "Assistant Minister S. Reljic reported that Croatian Army members were looting on a large-scale in Benkovac and apparently putting up armed resistance to military police members if they attempt to check them." And then there he has made a note saying: "Brigadier Biskic." Now isn't it correct that you telephoned him on 7th August and told him that Assistant Minister Reljic had reported this to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I find it very difficult to comment upon the contents of private diaries. However if --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I'm not asking you to comment. I'm just asking you, either you called General Lausic on 7th August and made -- told him about this matter or not.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered your question, and I said that I do not recall the date. It was a very specific answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recall the telephone conversation? I'm not asking about the date now. First, let me ask, do you recall being informed by the assistant minister, Mr. Reljic, that military personnel were committing crimes in Benkovac? And when -- and attempts to prevent resulted them in threatening with arms?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall. There were a lot of telephone conversations at the time, so I can't remember this particular one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you -- you don't recall telephoning Mr. Lausic and having a discussion about crimes in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I will withdraw that. That was a superfluous question, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Reljic is the assistant minister in charge of SUP; isn't it? That's Service for Protection of Constitutional Order. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have D46, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you will see on the screen, Mr. Moric, your letter to Mr. Lausic dated 10th August where you reported to him that: "Cases are being noted of individual Croatian Army members on liberated territory stealing movable property, burning houses and killing the cattle that strays around the area. "In addition, in some places there is a lack of cooperation at check-points and roadblocks." Now, when you sent this letter to General Lausic, was there some response, a positive response, to this? Did the situation improve or did they -- did you receive any kind of response from General Lausic that indicated the matter was being attended to? Or did the situation improve on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, Madam Prosecutor, whether I received an answer. At the time we had frequent communications, and I don't remember that I received any answer, which does not exclude the possibility that I did receive an answer. I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric, what you have testified here in terms of these interactions is between yourself and Mr. Lausic. Now, at any time, did you discuss these problems with your minister, Mr. Jarnjak?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, I don't understand which problem specifically you're referring to, the ones mentioned in the letter?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you used the term "problems," I'm referring to the terms -- I'm referring to crimes committed by military personnel that you have been discussing with General Lausic. Did you discuss that with your minister, Minister Jarnjak? Did you tell him or was there a discussion that crimes are being committed, and it's rampant, and some of the perpetrators are in military uniforms? Was that discussed with the minister?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, of course. The minister had to be informed of the trends in the state of security in the area. I did inform him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did the minister at any stage inform you in the course of those discussions that the matter would be raised with the Ministry of Defence, or the President? Or are you aware that the minister had in fact raised these concerns with the Ministry of Defence -- or the minister of defence, or the President, or both of them?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did discuss the issue. I know that the minister was concerned over the possible course of events. I know that he discussed the issue frequently with the minister of defence. I don't know if he was in communication with the President of the Republic. However, the logic would indicate that he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that -- that: "I know that he discussed the issue frequently with the minister of defence." Did he ever discuss with you what the response of the minister of defence was, in relation to the crimes being committed by members of the military?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, the response was that the head of the military police, the chief of the military police and I, should step up our efforts toward stabilizing security.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now when you say in principle the response was, did the minister tell that you that that was the response of the minister of defence, or are you just saying in a more logical term this was the response? Did the minister at any time tell you that when this concern was raised with the minister of defence, his response was that you and the head of the military police, chief of the military police should step up efforts?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, when I said in principle, I meant as a rule. Always when this was discussed, the minister's intention was that the military police and the Ministry of the Interior should do everything they could possibly do in professional terms in order to stabilise the situation. That's what I meant by saying in principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I want to find out what you knew as a fact not as a rule. Was it ever conveyed to you by Mr. Jarnjak that when he raised these concerns with the minister of defence, his response was that you and Mr. Lausic should step up security? Was that conveyed to you by the minister, Mr. Jarnjak?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, I don't know if he said it in so many words, but it was unequivocally clear that this was what was expected.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have D48, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, a week after you wrote your letter dated 10th August, you have raised this concern again with General Lausic. Now, obviously you're having to reiterate the issue again with General Lausic because a week after your previous letter the matter has not been satisfactorily resolved. So instead of raising the matter again with General Lausic, who obviously has not proved to be too effective, didn't you think of raising this concern with another source, or perhaps through the minister, raising this matter and trying to resolve it through another channel?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter was sent following daily contacts with Mr. Lausic. In answer to your question, I can say that channels or routes other than a more efficient cooperation between the civilian and military police did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, from what I understand, when you say this letter followed after daily contact with General Lausic, so as I understand it, at least from the 10th August, you have been in daily touch with General Lausic. And then on 17th August you write to him: "It is apparent from reports submitted by police stations" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I certainly object to that characterisation. That's not what the witness said: At least from 10th August he had daily contact with Lausic, that's not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me just rephrase, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now we see, Mr. Moric, a letter sent by you to General Lausic on 10th August. Now, you just referred to daily contact with General Lausic. Did you have daily contact with General Lausic from 10th August up until you wrote this letter to him on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if that was really the case, if it was on a daily basis at the time. In that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you -- you just testified, Mr. Moric, that this letter was sent following daily contacts with Mr. Lausic. So can you tell the Trial Chamber when your daily contacts started prior to this letter?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyday contact started with the meeting of the minister of defence, the one that we discussed yesterday. It did not happen every day. It depended on whenever a problem would emerge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Going to this letter, Mr. Moric, you report to Mr. Lausic that: "It is apparent from reports submitted by police stations and police administrations that cases of houses being burned down and other people's property being stolen are recorded on a daily basis in the Territory liberated in the Storm operation." Now, you said the reason that this matter could not be addressed is because of lack of cooperation between the military police and civilian police. Now, going by the two documents, D46 and D48, these two documents, your letter sent on 10th and letter sent on 17th, you have been raising this issue with Mr. Lausic for at least one week by 17th August. Didn't it occur to you that perhaps, as Mr. Lausic had not proven to be effective, you should try another method, perhaps address the issue with another source?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Prosecutor, I didn't say that the problem was big because of the poor cooperation with the military police but because the military police evidently had difficulties of such a nature that we, in the civilian police, did not have, or had to a much lesser degree. However, there was no other way, other than having the civilian police and military police cooperate on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I have D48, please. D48.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now following your letter of 17th August, you issued -- I'm sorry D49. My apologies, Mr. Registrar. You issued your 18th August order which has been discussed in court already. Now, as I understand your testimony to be, Mr. Moric, what you said was that in issuing this order, your expectation was that crimes committed prior to 18th August will be investigated after the situation had been brought into control. That's how I understood your testimony. I'm referring to transcript page 25563. Now, if that's the case, why didn't you mention that fact in this order? Why didn't you just, instead of giving a general order such as this, what you say is the meeting must be informed of the decision that cases of torching of houses and illegal taking away of people's movable property that have hitherto occurred will not be operatively investigated, but a stop must be put to cases of this type as of today. Now, why didn't you just add a proviso saying, once the matter is brought under control, investigate the crimes committed prior to 18th August retroactively, or some indication to your subordinates that those crimes were to be investigated after the matter is brought under control? Why didn't you mention that in your order?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please have the second page of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could have ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, the documents we discussed yesterday -- last week clearly show that I was in charge of the ordinary uniformed police and prevention, as provided for by the decree on the organisation and manner of work of the Ministry of Interior. Therefore, prevention was my job. As you can see, this document does not mention crime police, because, according to the structure, I am not in charge of that branch. This document has to do with the change of tactics of work employed by the ordinary police. It was to be done in such a way that policemen would not be kept lingering in the areas where, unfortunately, arson and looting had already been committed. Rather, they were to be fully engaged in the prevention of a spate of undesirable events, which does not preclude the crime police from acting in the areas where earlier incidents occurred. Besides, the context of the letter clearly shows that crime-scene investigations would continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric, now, if your position is that you were not involved in -- your police forces were not involved in crime investigation, what is the benefit or the purpose of your order in paragraph 2? What -- can you tell Trial Chamber exactly how you were getting additional resources in telling the fundamental police that crimes committed prior to 18th August would not be investigated? Now you said -- you used the word that they would not be lingering the in areas of -- where there had been already arson. As I understand your testimony, in -- by paragraph 2, what you're doing is, taking away the fundamental police who would have conducted the on-site investigations to -- towards prevention. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just on the form, Mr. President. I object to the comments by counsel beforehand, because I don't know for the purposes of the witness, but I do, if you look at the question and answer that goes for some -- excuse me, the question that goes for some 15 lines, the form of it is extremely confusing and unfocussed, and then we move to an additional question at the end. So just in practice, Mr. President, if we could ask the counsel to just ask a specific question and forestall the commentary prior to that, I think it would be helpful to all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I must say that it's not uncommon in this courtroom to hear this kind of questions being preceded by comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I'm -- it should not become practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will rephrase. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you inform the Trial Chamber, Mr. Moric, as to exactly how you intended to benefit, or what was the purpose of -- I don't want to use the word "purpose." How exactly did you intend crime prevention to be benefitted through not investigating crimes committed prior to 18th August? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while ago when answering your question, I explained precisely at that point. In other words, ordinary uniformed policemen would not be kept in the vicinity of the homes that had unfortunately already been looted, destroyed or torched, because the crime police will -- not because the crime police would need the assistance of ordinary policeman, but, rather, that the ordinary policemen would be engaged in the prevention of new crimes of such type, whereas, the assistance that the ordinary police would provide in the investigations that would be conducted was to be provided as soon as a state of a security was enforced. I think that the document indicates this quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said ordinary police would not be kept in the vicinity of the homes. When you use the word "kept," what you're talking about is the involvement of ordinary police in the on-site investigation, isn't it, securing the site, securing the evidence? That's what you're referring to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the following situation. Where there is an area with a number of such homes that need to have police presence until such time as the crime police teams arrive, in order to do their job. In other words, I'm referring to the obligation of the ordinary police to provide security to crime scenes. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, now, you remember in the examinations you testified when - in fact a question from the Bench - that you were asked as to how many members of the fundamental police are required to conduct an on-site investigation, and you said three for a case of arson. You gave numbers. And those numbers are based on probably - and you could correct me if I'm wrong - on the type of work they have to do at the on-site investigation, in securing the site, collecting the evidence. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't provide accurate figures. I think I gave what were average figures. His Honour asked me about what the average was. It was difficult to speak in other terms in the specific cases, so what I gave was a figure on average.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the question was about numbers, whether average numbers or -- so you're responding to a question which was not put to you, because Ms. Mahindaratne did not ask you about accurate numbers. I think that's clear for everyone. May I ask one question, since we have this document now on our screen anyhow. This order is addressing the police administrations, very generally. Would that include the crime police in those police administrations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would not include the crime police, because chiefs of police administrations knew that I was in charge of ordinary police and prevention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, second, on the second page of this document, not to investigate the earlier crimes, but then it continues giving clear instructions on, that on-site investigations have to be conducted, that should be agreed, after every case if the military police wouldn't do it, it would be the civilian police to do it alone. That sounds very much as clear instructions on what the crime police, crime section would have to do, because, on-site investigations, apart from the support from the -- from general police officers seems to be specifically the task of the crime police, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, ordinary police provides assistance in this sort of duty, and the document relates to these duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, at least you say, Because I was not in charge of the crime police, everyone would have understood that despite the fact that not the support is specifically addressed but a lot of other things as well, whether or not to investigate, whether on crime investigation should take place; if not, that everyone would have understood that your letter was limited only to the ordinary police supporting in these tasks. Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. Misetic has a translation issue on the transcript if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would first is it directly my question. If not, then I'd rather first have an answer. Mr. Moric, just look at me and -- instead of to the Defence and answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. Yes, that's how it should be understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Translation issue, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so that the Chamber is aware, in the Croatian he said something that was interpreted as, I did not give accurate numbers. I think there may be a different interpretation there that might have been more in the context of what the witness was trying to convey with the word that he used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When asked by Ms. Mahindaratne on you giving numbers, you started your answer by saying: "I did not give ..." What kind of numbers? Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant was that I didn't give precise numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, going back to my question, those numbers, and I'm not talking about precise, you know, just general numbers that you gave, were on the basis of the tasks that the fundamental police would have to do in an on-site investigation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Superfluous question, Ms. Mahindaratne. If you go through in detail about the questioning, it is how many people do you neat for this, for that, et cetera. Of course, is there security, was one of them, apart from the -- the specialists who would investigate the crime. So, therefore, could you please focus on -- on what really is in dispute, because approximately 30 per cent of your questions are about matters which are so obvious. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in taking away, when you -- when you -- by this order in paragraph 2, you diverting those sources, the fundamental police involved in on-site investigations towards prevention. Now, didn't it perhaps occur to the Ministry of Interior, perhaps one way to address the situation would have been to use crime police who -- personnel who were involved in tasks other than crime investigation during this period towards crime investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, it may be an interpretation issue. But I'm really not sure that I understood your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither did I, Mr. Moric. Could you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, are you aware as to what the priority tasks for the crime police were in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand why. In the aftermath of anything the tasks of the crime police have always been the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, are you aware that after the liberation a substantial number of crime police personnel were used for purposes of interviewing prisoners of war in the collection centres and also in searching and investigation -- investigating mass graves where persons of Croat ethnicity were buried? Are you aware that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we have a cite for that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum's -- I'm referring, for the record, to the testimony of Mr. Kardum, transcript 9306, 9290, and 9400. Also P896, paragraph 41. I could cite -- read them out, if necessary, Mr. President. I have those here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's split the question. Were you aware that crime police were used for purposes of interviewing those who were, I take it, suspected of rebellion, their activities in the rebellion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was aware of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second question, Ms. Mahindaratne, was about ... And please put the second part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now was it ever considered within the Ministry of Interior that perhaps one way to resolve the situation of shortage of personnel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second part of your question was about mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is, of course, a different category. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you also involved that the -- the primary task or the priority task of the crime police during this period, after liberation, was to search and investigate mass graves, in which persons of Croat ethnicity were buried?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me whether I knew that that was a priority?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether you were aware if that was in fact the priority task of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that. Because I also believed that that was not the priority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, there seem to be two questions. First, were you involved that the crime police did participant in the investigation of mass graves, in which Croats had been buried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what proportion of the time was spent on that task, what percentage of the crime police, or what percentage of their time was spent on these kind of investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you an answer to the question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Since you don't know, Mr. Moric, I will not pursue that issue any further. To a question from the Bench -- or just before -- let me just cite what you said. In relation to your order of 18th August, you responded to question, several questions, and I will read out what the Presiding Judge said: Yes, at least you say because I was not in this charge of the crime police. Everyone would have understood that despite the fact that not the support is specifically addressed but a lot other things as well whether or not to investigate, whether on crime investigation that should take place, that everyone would have understood that your letter was limited only to the ordinary police supporting in these tasks. Is that how I have to understand your answer? And unfortunately, you haven't responded to that question, because there was an interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the answer was given after the interruption and was in the affirmative. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you confirm that, Mr. Moric. And then, again, on this order, yesterday, you said that -- this is what you said: "There is not a single document. And no one from police administration asked what this was about. And if they believed that this was incorrect professionally or legally, they were duty-bound to warn me that I was requesting something that was not professionally or legally proper. So it was clear from our daily communication what this was all about and what the intentions were." So your testimony here is, Mr. Moric, that your subordinates understood your 18th August order in the context that you say you issued it. Now, would you be surprised if you were told that your subordinate officers testified here, in fact, Mr. Cetina testified in these proceedings, and this is what he had to say about your order, and I will read the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page number, please, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Transcript page 23589, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You say: "I don't recall discussing it with anyone ..." - that is your order - "... but I was not bound by that item. The Law on interior states that once I receive an official order which would be legal, I am under no obligation do implement it." In fact, at page 23415 there was a discussion about this order between the Bench and Mr. Cetina. And he said: "In a certain way it is not in fact in accordance with the law." And he was asked again: "So in a certain way it a violation of the law?" "In a way, yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the counsel put this in context because the questions in that regard, with regard to immunising for prior crimes, not for the order per se. If we go back through and look at the context of that entire conversation as well as Your Honours' questions of Mr. Cetina, it is clearly talking about whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, we're not going to tell exactly what the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I know, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you ask, if you invite Ms. Mahindaratne to give the context, then the same applies as I said before, which is that if you give unclear context, then that would trigger further questioning, whereas if you want to have the right answer right away, as I said before, it is always wise to give the context. Ms. Mahindaratne, there's a clear invitation --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Moric, the reference by Mr. Cetina to the illegal order is in relation to your order in paragraph 2, where it says that crimes before 18th August should not be investigated. That was the matter that was being discussed and not the order in its entirety. So this is what Mr. Cetina said, and there is also evidence here by another member of the Ministry of Interior, and I can't go into details of what he said because he testified under protective measures, Mr. Moric, where this order, that particular order in paragraph 2, not to investigate crimes before 18th August was described by him as a flagrant mistake. And this is transcript reference T5845, going up to 546? So, Mr. Moric, are you surprised that your subordinate officers in fact had not understood your order in the context that you say you issued it?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I am, indeed, surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, your reference to 5845 for Mr. Cetina's --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President that was the second witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the second witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina's would be 23415 and 23589.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I once again object. And if we look at the individual page that is cited by counsel, and I address, Mr. President, you to page 23411, Mr. Cetina's testimony, and if we look at lines 18 to 16 [sic] we can again -- I don't really -- excuse me, 8 to 16. I don't want to get ahead of myself, but I ask if we can contextualise this conversation with that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne may accept your invitation or you can deal with the matter in the further examination of the witness. Ms. Mahindaratne, I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't believe I have cited out of context, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's clear you do not accept the invitation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I have document D595, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, while that is coming up, Mr. Moric, I just want to ask you. In fact to a question from the Bench on this order. You said that you did not in fact issue a -- an order after the 18th August order, asking your subordinates to now go back and investigate those crimes committed prior to 18th August. So in that context, since you did not issue an order now to retroactively investigate those crimes, how did you expect your subordinates to react, you know, you expected them to spontaneously on their own decide, now this is the time to start investigating those crimes? Or did you expect them to individually do it? Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber how you expected your subordinates to resume investigation of crimes committed before 18th August?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, this would follow up from the technology of the police work. If the police, by way of their everyday work or receive information that a house had been plundered or set on fire, and then if the fundamental police had arrived on site, this would have been registered as a security event in the police administration in the area of which the event had happened. And if then an order is issued to change the tactics of the work of the police and if the police are removed from the area in order to boost the prevention of any new events, then the previous event had already been recorded, and it had already initiated all the subsequent procedures and actions prescribed by the law. That's why we are faced with the fact that criminal reports for crimes committed prior to the 18th were submitted any time after the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Moric, just moving on to one other matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have D -- oh, you already have that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The document on the screen, Mr. Moric, you're familiar with it. Those are the minutes of the meeting that took place in Plitvice on the 15th of September. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could have a minute, Mr. President. If could you go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, do you note, Mr. Cetina's statement there? He reports that: "... the emphasise on that fact that the biggest part of that area had been occupied. The situation in this area ... he divided into three stages." The first stage, stay of the HV professional unit [sic]. Second stage, stay of parts of the units which burnt houses and threatened with arms, and if tried to be prevented from committing crimes. And the third stage is stay of civilians which were taking property away on a massive scale.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now -- and he says: "He has also assessed the cooperation of the military police as unsatisfactory due to the insufficient number of military policemen." "Chief of Knin police administration agreed with the reply [sic] by Mr. Cetina and assessed the situation as satisfactory, considering these circumstances." Now, Mr. Moric, here's a meeting where you're present, members of the military police administration are present. And a report is made by a chief of a police administration that crimes are being committed by members of the HV and attempts to prevent that is being addressed -- responded to with arms, which is a serious issue, in terms of security. Now, did you ever consider raising this with the Ministry of Defence, or did you at least tell your minister that perhaps it was time to raise the matter with the Ministry of Defence without constantly addressing it with Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for individual cases involving armed threats among people who sported the visual identity of the Croatian Army or were, indeed, soldiers, there were such cases at that time. And the only way to remove that problem was to cooperate with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. But you said that, Mr. Moric, now from -- we have seen your attempt from 10th August, and this is the 15th September, over five weeks, clearly the cooperation with military police has not worked which is why the situation is not as it should be by this stage. Didn't it occur to you that perhaps your efforts so far has not yielded results?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm always listening with one ear here and then with the other ear to Mr. Kehoe, and then -- yeah. If I would like you to make a pause, I'll ask you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I finished my question. I was waiting for a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne -- Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question that came up was whether or not this was being raised, the issues were being raised with the Ministry of Defence, if the document itself is a joint meeting between the Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Defence. It's a -- the document that's on the screen is a document from the Ministry of Defence of the military police administration. So I'm a bit confused concerning the issue of raising this with the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my question was whether it was raised with the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Kehoe, where you said the matter was whether -- first of all, I think the question was about not whether it was done or not, but whether it was considered to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you look at page 30, line 3, we're talking about the Ministry of Defence. Doesn't say the minister, it says the Ministry of Defence. And then he says it again, Or did you at least tell minister that perhaps it was time to raise the matter with the Ministry of Defence ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First I was -- as a matter of fact, it's my recollection from listening to Ms. Mahindaratne that she referred to the minister of defence, but I could be mistaken there. But, of course, if you say instead of addressing it with Mr. Lausic, then, of course, you would expect the level higher up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of precision and clarity my -- my confusion I would assume, if it is being translated to the witness as Ministry of Defence, he may be a bit perplexed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this witness, first of all, Mr. Kehoe, has shown several times that if anything is unclear to him, that he immediately asks attention for that. And the question was not whether it was raised, but whether it was considered. That was at least how I understood your question. Mr. Moric, did you consider to raise the matter with the minister of defence instead of to continue discussing the matter with Mr. Lausic, at the level of Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Lausic was the relevant address for me. I didn't think about ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Taking it up higher. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, unfortunately, if I had addressed the higher level, they would have referred me to a lower level. The level that was actually the operative level and the one in charge of those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say that's the reason why you didn't raise it with the minister. Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm looking at the clock. I said that the scheduling issue would be dealt with later this morning. The Chamber would like to do it before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that we have a moment to think about matters that may be raised. For this reason, Mr. Moric, your break starts already now. We deal with a matter totally unrelated. Could you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The scheduling issue to be raised, who's going raise it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. As it refers to the beginning of the next week, that means from 14th up to 18th of December, we are preparing to call Witness Tomislav Penic on the very beginning of the week. But due to yesterday's telephone conversation, it would be impossible for him to come that week. But only after the winter recess. Therefore, we just calculated our witnesses, and suggest that we instead of Mr. Penic on the beginning of next week, we could call Ms. Bagic who was expected to testify after the winter recess. And with that proposal, we address the OTP, and got an answer that they are not, let's me put it this way, they are not agreeing with our proposal. So I am afraid if we just postpone the testimony of Mr. Penic on the beginning of next week, we will have a gap of the witnesses of, let's say, two days at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there are two questions. If you wouldn't call Mrs. Bagic, that would cause a delay, unless there would be any other witness that could fill that gap. In that case, there would be no additional delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have in mind that solution as well. But we simply cannot find some replacement for that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then next question is what is there to oppose the rescheduling of Mrs. Bagic from early January until the last few days of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. A lot of sympathy for the Defence position in relation to scheduling of the witnesses. That's very difficult, especially at the end when you don't have many more options. We -- I have said a couple of times, we have written e-mails on that, that there was an undertaking by the Defence in relation to the two witnesses they wanted to add, one of them, Ms. Bagic, to call them at the end of their case, and just distributed this morning, Mr. Kuzmanovic's undertaking that the last two witnesses in the case would be called either in the last two week -- in the last week before the holiday break, or if we go long, after the break. That's on the 13th November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I have the literal text of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can read it out: "Dear Stefan, you have received the Bagic statement with the filing, which wasn't the case. If you don't have it, let us know and it will be sent to you today. I will e-mail you the Watts [phoen] CV separately. You will get his report shortly. Both witnesses, if they are called will be the last two witnesses in the case, meaning, either the last week before the holiday break, or if we go long after the break. Let me know if you have any questions. Thanks. Best, Tom." 13th November. And there were a number of conversations with the Defence confirming that this was certainly our position. The next issue is that as we all know that spot in the week before Christmas was reserved for Witness Baric, the expert witness, and again, we have conversation on him. I have not heard any formal undertaking by the Defence to withdraw him or not. That was the issue, why there is a space now before Christmas. In relation to us being ready or not to call Ms. Bagic, based on the undertaking by the Defence in their original motion dated, I think, 10th November, to add the two witnesses, we organised our resources and the person who is most familiar with these difficult legal issues is not prepared to start next week for -- for various reasons. That's the reason why we would insist that the Markac Defence fulfil its commitment to call Ms. Bagic after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do understand that, initially it was announced that she would testify either late December or early January. Then, in the motion in which it was requested to add Witness MM-026, I think it was put that the amendment of the witness list would not result in an unreasonable delay of the proceedings, and any issues concerning preparation time needed for the cross-examination of the witness and conduct of the necessary investigations, that could be met by scheduling the witness to appear at the end of the Markac Defence case. Now, I -- did you raise at any time, because I did understand that from your answer to the motion to add, among others, among another, Witness MM-026, that you didn't raise anything, that only if it would be in January. And, therefore, I'm wondering, we start with the position, either late December/early January, then there's a motion saying if there are any issue, then that could be met by scheduling, and then we get a response saying, without any reservation, that there's no objection to adding Witness MM-026 to the Markac witness list. That -- is there any specific moment where you say, It could not be done before the winter recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be done in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just as a practical matter that may actually accommodate both sides, I note that she's scheduled for the last day that we are to sit before the break, which I think is 16th. And the Markac Defence has asked for three or four sessions of direct examination which would allow us then to have her direct examination and then -- she, anyway, would have had to come back for cross-examination, so perhaps that's an accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Gotovina Defence as mediator.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's an option which I will discuss internally. In addressing your points, Mr. President, we did rely on the representation from the Defence that she would be called last. I agree that we did not specifically state in our response, Yes, we want to hold you to the fire in relation to that. But the first moment we were told, I think in an e-mail by Mr. Rendulic, that this witness might be called earlier. I immediately responded by e-mail, went to the Defence, discussed it with them, to tell them that this was not our understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier is an ambiguous expression in this respect, because earlier can mean not the last of the case. But earlier could also mean earlier in time, that is, which month. And I do understand that it has been an option on from the beginning that she would testify perhaps as the last witness in December, and that the Prosecution should have been ready for that and has not made any reservation in this respect. Now let me be very concrete, Mr. Waespi. Is it that this preparation takes so much time, or is it simply that one of your team members who would deal with the matter is not present?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's a combination. And Ms. Gustafson who will deal with Mrs. Bagic is also involved in the 54 bis filing preparations and the closing brief, and so on. Again we are not different from the Defence position, the resources are scarce. But there is a lot of scheduling, a lot of thinking about how to respond to these many issues, and that's why we -- we jumped on -- on the issue of reserving the testimony, the important testimony of Ms. Bagic to -- to -- after -- at the end of the Defence case, whenever that it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it is not physical unavailability, but being occupied with other matters, and -- I suggest, that, Mr. Misetic, that you suggest to the parties that they would accept your mediation, and if there is no positive result, then, of course, the Chamber will rule on the matter. We have a break, and we resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, from what I know of ADR, it is not always the mediator to be blamed for not being successful because mediation focuses on the activity of the parties themselves. The Chamber is informed that your efforts for which we thank you, has failed. The parties are invited to briefly, in a very short or for you, as the mediator, to tell us exactly what the -- where the problem seems to be problematic. I wouldn't spend too much time on it in court, but -- Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't think the mediator talked to me over the break, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, the mediation -- what I learned from ADR is that at least the mediator should speak to each of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but learned also in my experience that when one of the parties has taken a position that in advance, will make it a pointless exercise to speak to the other, then -- that's why I avoided it, Mr. President. In short, the problem was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I wanted to deal with the matter in further detail in -- in Court at this moment. I was about to invite, to inform in a short e-mail what apparently the problem is, but hearing that the parties have not even met, I would suggest that in the next break, and, of course, we couldn't expect any better result without your assistance, Mr. Misetic, but let's see whether direct contact between the parties as a last ultimate resort for this problem to be resolved, whether that works. If not, the Chamber will rule. And then, the Chamber would really prefer to receive perhaps from the parties, then, in less than half an A-4, a short message to say, This was an obstacle for this party, that was the obstacle for the other party, so that we know exactly what the real problem is. And that's -- yes, I -- I tried desperately not to further bore Mr. Moric with the matter, but -- and to spend as little time on court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have just one sentence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There is no obstacle on our part at all. So we will follow the ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will be ready to start the examination-in-chief and do cross after the break, if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that seems not to be -- I'm informed that that would, for one reason or another, would not work, and that's the reason why I invite you to sit again together and whether or not with a cup of coffee. Let's continue, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, you would offer yourself as a mediator. It's appreciated. No, no, I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we proceed, I kindly ask for your assistance. When Madam Prosecutor asked me about my 18th of August document and called its legality into question, I expected that I would have an opportunity to provide the Chamber with the facts which indicate that legality is not to be questioned. However, we moved onto a different document in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, what happened is that Mr. Kehoe wanted to put the matter in a context in which the several stages of the testimony of the witness who expressed himself on whether or not it is legal or not to give any instructions not to investigate, and we do understand from your testimony that you look at it in a bit different way, is not to never investigate but to leave it until the moment where there's a time and an opportunity to investigate the matter, which, at that time was not specifically addressed and which may have an impact on any assessment of the legality. But I take it that Mr. Kehoe will further deal with the matter. And if not, then you'll have an opportunity to briefly address. But then in -- in a limited context. You will have an opportunity to express yourself. Because I do understand that you're a bit concerned by testimony which would say that your order was an illegal one, that seems to be your concern, which I could understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, just before we go off this document, I just want you to take note of two entries here, about which I will ask you a question later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could move, Mr. Registrar, to the English page, page 4, and the Croatian page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There is a record of what Captain Matanic, commander of the 72nd [sic] Military Police Battalion said at this meeting where you were present. In the second paragraph he says: "He mentioned the example of Donji Lapac where even MUP members were setting houses on fire." And then I just want you to take note of that, Mr. Moric, because I will ask about it later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could move to English page 6 and Croatian, which is on page 4, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then you see your concluding remarks, Mr. Moric. It is recorded here: "Mr. Moric emphasised that the shift of responsibility led nowhere. He expressed his positive opinion to [sic] reports by Messrs. Cetina, Dasovic, and Matanic. "He also supported remarks made by General Lausic and said that we had an equal responsibility for all citizens of the Republic of Croatia regardless of their nationality. The fact is that at the moment everybody is engaged in looting - from civilians to representatives of civilian authorities, and to the members of civilian and military police. The most important thing is to perform one's duties in a professional manner and differentiate from the personal attitude." I just wanted to bring to your notice your concluding remarks because I will ask a question about it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have document number D3483.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You will see in a moment, Mr. Moric, your order dated 13 September August [sic]. I'm sorry, 13th September. And whereby, you have withdrawn police forces, the resources.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could go to the top of the page so that Mr. Moric could see the document in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, can you follow the document, Mr. Moric. It's dated 13 September, two days before the Plitvice meeting. You order as follows: "On 15th September, 1995, withdraw separate police units in order to reduce the number of police officers, as follows: "Krapina Zagorje police administration shall withdraw 61 officers from Knin. "Primorje-Gorski Kotar police administration shall withdraw 50 officers from Gracac. "Zagreb police administration shall withdraw 63 officers from Korenica and 28 officers from Donji Lapac. "Split-Dalmatia police administration shall withdraw 50 officers from Vrlika. "And Karlovac police administration shall withdraw 20 officers from Krnjak. "After withdrawal, the officers shall be assigned to their regular tasks."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if could you move to the next page on the English, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You say: "After withdrawal of the determined number of officers, the number of officers that remains there to help shall continue reducing by 15 per cent per month - during regular replacement of officers." Now, Mr. Moric, I'm trying to understand this. Now, on the 15th itself, we see that meeting where there is a report of parts of units, military units committing crimes, and when it's tried to be prevented, reacting with arms. There is a military police officer who has reported at that meeting that there -- that members of MUP are burning in Donji Lapac. And you, yourself, have concluded the meeting by saying that everybody, including members of the military police and the civilian police, are looting. Now, in this context, why are you withdrawing your police forces from the liberated areas when you in fact testified already that one of the problems you faced was shortage of personnel? How do you reconcile the two positions?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, at the meeting held on the 15th of September at Plitvice, a fraction of the management of the civilian and military police analysed the events that had transpired by that date. In other words, individuals reported on the occurrences, the arising problems, and responses to them. At that stage, we were gradually stabilizing the situation, though we were not fully in control yet. On the other hand, we had other security risks that had to be addressed, the ones that we discussed last week, such as security of the lengthy state border, terrorist attacks, which, unfortunately, were directed at vital infrastructure, the population in the areas were -- that had just been liberated were vulnerable in terms of property being damaged, and this happened, and we were proceeding to gradually man the police stations at the liberated territories at a pace of 15 per cent a month. The procedure went on for the subsequent six months.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, now you said that at the time meeting the situations was analysed, and we were gradually, at that stage you were gradually stabilizing the situation. Now, I didn't see that from the minutes, Mr. Moric, because you -- in fact, your concluding remarks are that "everybody is looting." That's how you finished the meeting, and you conclude that meeting. You testified over and over again and you informed this Trial Chamber that one of the greatest problems you faced was shortage of personnel to address crimes in the liberated area. That's on the one hand. But, on the other hand, we saw yesterday, you withdrew Mr. Buhin who was a specialist in crime prevention and replaced him with an expert in traffic matters. And then you also, in addition to that, reduce forces. Now, to me, your actions at that time somehow is not consistent with the actions of somebody wanting to address a crimes, wanting to really prevent the crimes. How do you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, you are focussed on one problem, which took up most of my time as well. The state of security throughout the area and the prevention of crime throughout the country was also my problem. On the other hand, as I put it a moment ago, the intention was to gradually reduce the police personnel over a period of six months by manning the police structures in the newly liberated areas at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. But what we see in this order, Mr. Moric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could we just first try to establish exactly what we're talking about. The withdrawal of the determined number of officers, were those officers who came from elsewhere and had been called to help in the early stages of the liberated areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. They are the ones this is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you took out those who had come from elsewhere and were assisting in the early stages gradually; and, at the same time, you were recruiting police officers to strengthen the police organisation locally. That is, to man the strength of the police force in the area. Is that what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. That's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric, if you were manning, as you say, the police stations in the liberated area with new recruits, then what you're talking about is taking away the experienced personnel and replacing those resources with new recruits who are inexperienced, and thereby manning your police stations in the areas where the crimes were high with persons who are just new to the service. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mrs. Prosecutor, you're not right. That was not the intention, nor did this happen in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you explain how then did you replace these officers who were being withdrawn as we see in this order? We see numbers of officers being withdrawn. How and by what numbers did you replace them? Do you have any documentation to substantiate or to provide that information, or can you tell us right now?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is documentation in the Ministry of the Interior dating from that period, including the decision of the ministerial collegium, whereby assistant ministers for personnel financial affairs, and other matters provide their support to the process. Let me draw your attention to this fact. What is the area that these policemen are returning to? They are going back to Zagreb, Krapina, Rijeka, Split, Karlovac. In a word, to the areas where they normally reside and work and where, according to the labour law and other valid legislation they exercised all of their rights. It was impossible to keep them in the area all the time. It was reasonable for us to plan a gradual replacement of the personnel with individuals who would be permanently settled and work in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If could I just ask you one question based on that answer, Mr. Moric. Now, we see, according to this order, for example, if you take the first entry, The Krapina Zagorje police administration withdraw 61 officers from Knin. Is the replacement of those 61 officers immediate, or you just use the word gradual, or was the replacement gradual?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, let's try to understand what we have in front of us. On 15 September withdraw separate police units in order, and then we get the numbers. Then on the next page of this document it says: "After withdrawal of the determined numbers [sic] of officers, the number of officers that remained [sic] there to help shall continue reducing by 15 per cent per month during regular replacement of officers." So the document seems to be perfectly clear. Take out the 60, look at what remains, and then gradually withdraw 15 per cent every month of those remaining. So if talking about gradually, we start with a fixed number and then we continue gradually, at least I have difficulties in any way understanding in a different way. So the question, was it done gradually or not, is -- first of all, I think the document gives the answer. Whatever conclusions to be drawn, whether it would be fair, whether it would be -- but the system is set out with, in my view, extreme clarity in this document. And the question, was it done gradually is not, is -- seems to be confusing, rather than to add anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was really focussing on the determined number, the 61, and not the 15 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it says on the 15th of September withdraw 60 men, that seems not to be -- after withdrawal, then do it gradually every month. So, therefore, even in this respect, unless there's any reason to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it? On the 15th of September, take out 60 here, 80 there, whatever. After that, those remaining of those who came from elsewhere, reduce them by 15 per cent. I really have great difficulties in understanding that you would not understand this document in this way and that you're seeking clarification. Let's briefly ask. Mr. Moric, my interpretation of the document, is that -- you could confirm that that is what the document says. Whatever it's fair or unfair, or appropriate to do, or inappropriate to do, but is my understanding of what the document says right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
