utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've completely understood the matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, moving onto a completely different area, that is, your testimony about General Cermak's --

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, can we just briefly go back to the minutes of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We will do that later on, Mr. Moric. I am under limited time. So -- we will go back to prior to -- before closing my examination. At this stage, I just want to address your testimony on what you said about General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could have document D494 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you, while this document is coming up - and you may not have seen that document or you may have seen it - have you seen any written orders issued by General Cermak to the Knin police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, I saw some of the documents at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say you saw some of the documents at a later date, was it during preparation for testimony here, or did you see it at any other place, any other time?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, in the context of my preparation for the testimony. I don't recall seeing them before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So the first time you saw written orders issued by General Cermak to the police was when the Defence showed you the documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the witness just said, Ms. Mahindaratne. I have not seen them before; I saw them when preparing. Try to use your time as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now at any stage, had members of the Knin police informed you that they had received orders from General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, are you familiar with this document that is on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an order. Yes, I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I didn't refer to as your order, Mr. Moric. Now, there is a -- some text at the bottom of the page. Is that your writing?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where did you see this document? You said you're aware of it. Did you receive this document? It is addressed to the Operation Povratak staff. Did you receive it at any stage?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that one of my associates showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in showing the document, in this letter, the query is: Please reply and confirm in writing the validity of the passes for civilian persons in question and that queries made by the -- Mr. Ivo Cipci, I believe, that is the chief of the Split-Dalmatia police administration. Was it you who made the query as to validity of the pass, or your colleague? Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I believe, if I can remember things well, that I ordered my associate to investigate the matter. Because when I saw that, the least I can say was that I was angry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Why were you angry?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because restrictions on the movement of people anywhere else but in the areas where combat is going on cannot be within the authority of either the army or the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I earlier told Ms. Mahindaratne that you had answered the question, but, looking at this document and talking about when you saw these documents, you said that you saw them in the context of your preparation for testimony. I don't recall seeing them before. Now, half a page later you say, I believe that it was shown to me by -- "I believe that one of my associates showed it to me." And then you say what orders you gave to investigate the matter, et cetera. These answers are not easy to reconcile, on the one hand saying I saw them during preparation for my testimony, and now you start explaining that you believe that it was shown -- Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I believe if we go back to the question on page 48, line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 48, 17. One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And 18 and 19. It may provide the source of confusion because it is directed towards Mr. General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well -- no, it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree with Mr. Kehoe that my question was specifically directed at a particular type of document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That's -- I was about to say, Ms. Mahindaratne, that I would not have told you that the witness had already answered the question. But, at present, I'll -- I'll refrain from any further comment. Yes, I think it would have been transparent, if, at page 49, line 11, you would have said, Now we move to a different type of document, or a different document, because there was no clear separation between the issue you addressed earlier and the issue you addressed now. But it's clear to me, and I think more careful reading on my side would have prevented me from making my last observation, not my earlier observation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Moric. If you could go back to -- you said you were angry because -- and let me just see. You said: "Because restrictions on the movement of people anywhere else but in the areas where combat is going on cannot be within the authority of either the army or the -- or the Ministry of Defence." So with whom were you angry, Mr. Moric? Who -- towards whom were [sic] your anger directed?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about the fact that somebody, whoever it may have been, came up with an idea that they might be doing things that they were not within their authority. Whoever it was, as I say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, there's a note here that says: "By checking through the Knin police, Colonel General Cermak will issue an order on the annulment of travel passes and free movement of civilians. It must come in writing from Ministry of Defence and the Republic of Croatia." Now who made that inquiry from the Knin police with regard to this matter? Was it you, or was it your associate who was attending to this?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of my associates did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If memory serves me well, it was Mr. Tomurad. He was the chief of the duty service sector. And that's how things were done. In terms of communication, we communicated with the duty service sector which was a regular procedure whenever we were faced with an operative problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, do you know if any representations were made to General Cermak in order to have these passes annulled? How was it brought about that General Cermak had either agreed or, you know, had undertaken to annul these passes? Can you tell the Trial Chamber as to what exactly transpired for this outcome.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't tell you exactly what my associate did, or I can't give you the whole scope of the actions that he undertook. But I can give you the end result.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, beyond this issue, were any other inquiries made from the Povratak staff, as to any other aspects of General Cermak's passes beyond asking whether it was valid. Was the Ministry of Interior asked for any qualifications as to what those passes or to -- against whom those passes could be used, or in relation to whom those passes could be used?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember. However, what comes to mind and what I can tell you for a fact is that, at that time, we, in the Ministry of Interior, understood that high officials or high officers of the Croatian Army could request for the issuance of some sort of passes or documents to that effect, and those documents would entitle either soldiers or civilians employed by the army to move freely through the areas and facilities used or occupied by the army or the Ministry of Defence. That's how we understood the matter at the time. We believed that the whole matter was restricted to such situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you another document, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could have -- well, before that, if you could go to the next page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, are you familiar with that pass? Have you seen that -- had you seen this pass before this document -- this letter reached you on 15th August?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen it before. I believe that this is a pattern, and I'm not sure that it was precisely this document that was attached to that letter, whether this was the form that was attached to that letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me call another document, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if I could have D496, please. I'm sorry, it should be D495. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, are you able to tell the Trial Chamber as to who wrote that entry at the bottom of this pass?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me to identify the author based on the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm just asking whether you are aware as to who wrote. If you're not aware, that's quite all right. I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could have D496, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, there is an inquiry, a request made from the same police administration that sent your previous letter to the ministry that we looked at, which was D494. And it said: "We ... send and admission to the liberated. We are very pressured by citizens and displaced persons who wish to visit liberated areas Knin and Drnis. We have been informed that the regular Split-Knin railroad line has been restored, which is being regularly announced through the media ... where citizens are informed that they have free transport on the said railroad line in the next ten days. This creates enormous pressure, both at valid checkpoints and in," if you could go to the next page, "... operation staffs because citizens feel that they can travel without any problems [sic] on the said train. "Please give us urgent directions as to how we should act in this newly developed situation." And on this same document --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could go back, Mr. Registrar, to the first page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- there is a handwritten note saying: "Call the Split-Dalmatia police administration and say that Cermak will annul the passes today." Now, isn't it correct, Mr. Moric, that the document we saw previously, where there was a note at the bottom saying through Knin police administration it was found out that Cermak -- General Cermak will annul the passes, that was connected to this request sent by the Split-Dalmatia police administration, is it the same day?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that this is about the request that came from the police administration. This document is about a normal train journey on a regular train service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, you have seen two documents, both sent by the same police administration to the Povratak staff on the same day, 15th August, on the same issue. One says that you need to make access to the liberated area -- you know, the civilians should be allowed unrestricted access. And the other issue is an inquiry about the validity of passes issued by General Cermak. And in relation to both documents there is a note that General Cermak would be cancelling the passes. So are you saying that these are two separate inquiries, or they're not connected? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Prosecutor, this is my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can I have document P509, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you seen this order, Mr. Moric, before prior to your preparations for the testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, on the same day, you have the very same day has 15th August 1995, General Cermak issues an order to the Knin police saying: "From 15th August, 1995, onwards allow civilians unhindered entry into the town of Knin at all check-points of the military and civilian police on all access roads to the town. "Permit civilians to enter the town of Knin without passes and carry out routine checks following the rules set out earlier." Now, you just said a little while ago that you were very angry that these restrictions of movement was being issued in an unauthorised manner. Did you have anybody raise that with General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam Prosecutor. At that time, when it comes to the thing that we have just discussed, I understood this as an idea, as an intention, and I realised that that idea and intention had been eliminated and amounted to nothing. So nothing came out of that idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I don't understand that answer, Mr. Moric. Let me just ask you this way. Do you agree with me that this order of General Cermak is connected to the -- the other two documents that we saw earlier on, which are sent to the Povratak staff by the Split-Dalmatia police administration? Isn't it pursuant to that inquiry that General Cermak issued this order?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember things properly, those documents bear the same date. As to their sequence, I don't know. I can only speculate. I can only speculate whether one thing preceded the other or the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. I don't want you to speculate. Mr. Moric, let me just show you one other document on this subject, and then I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could have P510, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you will see a document on the screen, Mr. Moric, which is dated 16 August, the day after this order was issued by General Cermak, and that is a document from the Knin police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric, were you aware of that sequence of events, where, after General Cermak issued his order of the 15th August, the Knin police issued an order implementing that? Were you aware of that sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Then would you agree with me, Mr. Moric, that you are not -- you have not been fully apprised, or you were not fully aware of the exact nature of the interactions between General Cermak and the Knin police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle. But it is obvious that in this particular data -- detail, I did not. I did not know that the head of the civilian police wrote this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we have an issue with the beginning portion in terms of the interpretation. Page 59, line 1, on my screen, which is page 58, line 25, on the centre LiveNote. If we could ask for clarification because I think it is inverted as to what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked, Mr. Moric, whether you were -- whether you would agree that you were not fully aware of the exact nature of the interactions between General Cermak and the Knin police. And then your answer started with, Yes. But could you please repeat what you added to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in principle. In principle, I was aware, but when it comes to this detail, the detail of this letter, I was not fully aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Detail of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, his answer is, In predictable I was informed of the nature of their relationship but not of the details. And the way it came out was that, yes, he agreed with Ms. Mahindaratne's assertion, which is not what he had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not fully aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to verify, you confirmed that, in general terms, you were aware of the interactions between General Cermak and the Knin police but not in detail. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was even more specific and clear when I said that I was not aware of this detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, going to another area. Mr. Kehoe questioned you about the jurisdiction of the civilian police over military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could have document D214.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I appreciate you may not have seen the document that is about to come on the screen. This is a meeting of the closed sessions of the government and you have the prime minister present there and several other cabinet ministers, including Mr. Jarnjak. And I just wanted to first show you, this is the cover page of the minutes so that you take notice of who was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if could I have D215.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm going to a portion of those minutes, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could go to -- in the English, page 2, and the Croatian, page 38.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just wanted to remind you that, in case you didn't take note, that this is a meeting on 5th October, 1995, in that -- in the English the second paragraph starting from last three lines. There's Minister Jarnjak saying: "... here at the closed sessions I have to say that I will try to get in touch with the minister of defence today to see if there is a lack of, or if there is an insufficient number of military police in that area" --

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian version is evidently -- has evidently got the wrong page on the screen, because I can't see what you are reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: sorry. I think have you it now, Mr. Moric. Did you note that? Let me just take you to the exact line. It's the third line from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could go down to the page, Mr. Registrar. There.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's just -- I'm starting halfway through his address: "... here at the closed sessions [sic] I have to say that I will try to get in touch with the minister of defence today to see if there is a lack of, or if there is an insufficient number of military police in that area that should be present, as there is a large number of military personnel, or at least persons wearing uniforms who do not wish to show their IDs to the civilian police."

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have the continuation of the text in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There you have it.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "They do not wish to cooperate" -- I'm sorry, they do not wish to show their IDs to the civilian police. "The civilian police have no jurisdiction over the military personnel. They do not wish to cooperate and we have problems because there is isn't a sufficient number of these people in that area, and therefore we ... ask for this." Now, Mr. Kehoe questioned you about this issue. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber exactly what the civilian police could do upon seeing a member of the military committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could have stopped and identified the individual to see if it was a soldier or a civilian who was abusing the uniform. Of course, I am assuming that the individual whom the civilian police wished to identify is not resisting the procedure. In the event that there is physical resistance, it is up to the civilian policeman to use his judgement as to whether he would use, and, if so, which sort of restraining means that he is authorised to use. If he resorts to the use of restraining equipment, and if it is an ascertained that the individual is, indeed, a member of the army, then the individual should be handed over to the care or the custody of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kehoe asked you this question. And then this is what you said in response. This is at transcript reference T-25724. You say: "However, at the time that we're talking about and considering the problems at the time, the situations that we were faced with most often were such that it was clear from the very beginning that these were military persons. So we didn't need the criminal processing to establish that these were military persons, and in that context I wanted to say that in such situation it was clear that the military police would be in charge of that from the start." Now, can you tell Trial Chamber what you meant by "it was clear from the very beginning that these were military persons." What were the factors that made it clear when you saw persons committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to a situation where a policeman would be faced with individuals who appeared to be members of the army. It can be a perplexing situation in the sense that one is uncertain whether the individual is, indeed, a soldier or not. Again, there could be situations where, undoubtedly, the individual concerned is a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you be a bit more specific, Mr. Moric, because I don't think you really answered my question.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said I was referring to a situation where a policeman would be faced with individuals who appeared to be members of the army, and it can be a perplexing situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question was what did you mean that in those it was clear from the beginning that the perpetrators were members of the HV? I'm asking to you clarify your response to Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just tried to give you an answer, Mrs. Prosecutor. If the policeman believed that the individual was, indeed, a soldier, and it was down to his own judgement, because he was experiencing the situation, the assessment he makes will be based on several elements before him; the visual appearance of the individual, the gear that he carries along, and similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just, while we're on this document, I just want you to also focus on another section, statement of the minister. This is at the same page, and you can follow it on page 40 of the Croatian document. The minister says: "Therefore, what we spoke about at the very start, that torching, blowing up, and then taking things away can be explained by folklore, well that was taking things away in a kind of way. Here again, at the closed session, I have to stay it in a legal sense that all and sundry signed all sorts of receipts, starting from war booty do stolen property, from the prefect, deputy prefect, offices, associations, mayors, all signed receipts on who has the right and what they have the right to take out. It has come to a situation in which people gained the impression and they can take" --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in the English if you could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "... they can take absolutely anything that belongs to anybody. This means that it was not only houses that belonged to Serbs that were plundered, houses that belong to Croats are now up for it, and that is a very serious problem. "Therefore, this is no longer a question of some kind of folklore. This is now the question of serious organised crime that we have been burdened with and that we have to solve." Now, as I understand the minister's statement here, his concern is that, at this stage, crimes have got so out of hand that houses belonging to Croats are now being plundered, and he considers that a serious problem. Now is that consistent with your own observations regarding the trends? And you -- since you said you were following the trends on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is common knowledge in the police practice that crime knows of no boundaries, including ethnic ones. We knew that from the start. When it comes to the plundering of abandoned, empty homes, the criteria news was not that of ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Moric. My question is the minister is saying, earlier on, the crimes were directed at Serb property, and now it has moved from Serb property to Croat property, and he says that is a serious problem. Now my question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, that is not what the transcript says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, would you please verify and see --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will read it again to you, Mr. Moric. It says: "It has come to a situation in which people gained the impression and they can take absolutely anything that belongs to anybody. This means that it was not only houses that belonged to Serb that were plundered; houses that belonged to Croats are now up for it, and that is a very serious problem." So my question is: is that consistent with your own observations, that the trend of crimes developed, initially the targeting was Serb houses, but at this stage when this conversation was taking place, it is now heading towards crimes being directed against property belonging to Croats. Is that how you saw the trend?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mrs. Prosecutor, but I think that I've just answered this question. From the beginning, we never stated that crime was confined within ethnic boundaries, but, of course, in view of the number of criminal incidents and the property on the other hand, unfortunately, most of the crime committed was to the detriment of owners who were ethnic Serbs but not exclusively so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, let me just ask you one last question, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have P494, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is moving into another area, Mr. Moric, which is an area you're familiar with, collection centres and reception centres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's P494.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now this document was in fact called up by Mr. Mikulicic, and you discussed this document with him. And this is what you said about the collection centres. This is at transcript reference 2554. "Thus the idea of reception or collection centres was to receive all categories of people and to provide all of them with the basic conditions fit for human beings. And also the intention was to interview all those people and then in keeping with their possibilities, their wishes allowed them to achieve their goals." Now is it correct, then, to understand that the collection centres and reception centres or reception centre, whatever you prefer to call them, received both the prisoners of war and the civilians? These two categories of people, all of them were held in the same premises. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm with any certainty, or deny the possibility, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, you are the person who set up these -- this system. In fact, we have the order right in front of the -- front of you. If you do not know how the system was operated, who would?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Prosecutor, I would have to read the entire document and see what it states in relation to prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Please do so. This is your own order, but please take your time and read it.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the rest of the text? Further down, please. Further down. Thank you. I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now are able to answer my question? I could repeat my question. My question was that, isn't it right that both civilians and prisoners of war, were these categories of people were accepted to these collection centres, in that both were taken in, into the same premises, to these collection centres?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The document requests that prisoners of war be separated from the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where -- where in this document do you see that prisoners of war be separated from the rest?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have page 2 first, and then perhaps 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if he could have page 2 first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page, please. The top of item 3. The top of the page, item 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can we just take, in the English, if you could -- you're referring to the paragraph that starts: "If it is established ..." Is that the -- "If is established that the person does not reside on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, the person will be confined to a special part of the collection centre along with other persons of the same status. Such person [sic] must be registered separately." Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try to assist, Your Honour. I see the confusion. The confusion obviously derives from the fact that one word which is in Croatian language mentioned before the person is not translated in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In Croatian language it states: [Interpretation] "If it is established that the person captured or person taken prisoner." [In English] And in English it states: "If it is established that a person."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, could you read out paragraph 3 loud, please, in Croatian. The paragraph you're pointing to us, can you read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "If it is established that the person taken prisoner does not reside or have a place of residence in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, it shall -- he or she shall be set aside and placed into a separate part of the collection centre with other persons holding the same status."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, the way I see it, there difference is you are asking that persons who do not reside on the territory be separated. Now you have in fact explained this in your testimony, and I can read you. This is at transcript page 25554, and I will read your entire answer about this document. You said: "As a result of that, those who wanted to stay in the Republic of Croatia would be issued with the appropriate documents and accommodated in such areas where their safety could be guaranteed. At the same time such places had to receive the former members of the paramilitary and para-police forces who had taken off their paramilitary uniforms and removed paramilitary insignia from their clothes and, thus, changed their visual identity. It was a notorious fact." Then you talk about a third category: "We knew from before that among them there were also people who were not citizens and nationals of the Republic of Croatia, who had never been citizens of Croatia, nor they had any ambition to become our nationals. The police -- at that time the penal law prescribed penalties for participation in armed rebellion. The police tasks, amongst others, was to collect information about any person who had committed that type of crime. The idea of reception or collection centre was to receive all categories of people and to provide all of them with the basic conditions for human being, and also the intention was to interview all those people and then in keeping with their possibilities, their wishes allowed them to achieve their goal." So this paragraph you are pointing to as your instruction to separate prisoners of war from civilians is not exactly what you -- what you claim to be, Mr. Moric. In fact it relates to persons who are not residents or, as you clarified to Mr. Mikulicic, who were never citizens of Croatia. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Prosecutor, unfortunately, I am not sure anymore if I understand your question fully. The reception centres were supposed to receive all persons who were in need of some sort of assistance, and almost everyone needed assistance at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne, not for the first time, we now hear about reception centres. The question that was put to you by Ms. Mahindaratne was about collection centres. Now, could we first verify whether there is any difference between sabirni centar and the reception centre you were just talking about. Mr. Kehoe, let me first --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, before the witness answers, if I may independently direct the Chamber to a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know they are different languages used in other documents, that's exactly the reason why I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's a little bit more specific. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's first -- I appreciate your assistance. Could we first hear the answer of the witness. You were asked to read a document about what is translated to us "collection centre," and which, in the original reads sabirni centar. Is that anything different as far as you are concerned with the centres you just mentioned, where everyone was supposed to be looked after in the appropriate way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, there was no difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the whole line of questioning, Ms. Mahindaratne, started with a relatively simple question. Whether both civilians and prisoners of war were received in these sabirni centar. Yes. Now, the witness said, yes, but they were separated. And I read that from paragraph B, under 3. Now in B, under 3, there was apparently an incomplete translation about the persons. But could we go back to what apparently was the issue, that how, from paragraph B, 3, as it appears on your screen at this very moment, how we could read from that paragraph that a distinction was made, a separation was made between prisoners and civilians, because we have now spent quite some time on establishing that apparently there was something about people residing on the territory or not residing on the territory, which, I would assume, is different from the distinction between civilians and prisoners. So could you first explain how, in paragraph B, 3, we can read that civilians and prisoners were separated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the text reads, or states, that first it needs to be established that the person was taken prisoner. Then it has to be determined whether the person has a place of residence in Croatia. And then it needs to be confined to a separate part of the centre with the persons holding the same status. So, number one, taken prisoner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It means that prisoners who have no residence on the territory of the Republic of Croatia should be separated and registered separately and should be placed in a special part along with other persons of the same status. That is, other persons without residence on the territory of the Republic. But that is a not a distinction between prisoners and civilians. It is two categories of prisoners. Those who are taken prisoner and who have no residence in Croatia should be put apart. That's at least how I read it, and I invite you again to indicate what in this text clearly establishes that prisoners were to be separated from civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. But as many times before, I believe we have a translation issue problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case, then the witness who has the original available will first give his answer, and I'm fully willing, unless my question is wrongly translated. If that's the case, I invite you, or at least if you think that my question is wrongly translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with all due respect, your question is wrongly in fact wrongly translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll rephrase it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But not due to your mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not talking about mistakes. Then I'll rephrase question, which avoids --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... No, Your Honour, let me put an end preposition. Just to establish what is the proper translation of the Croatian word "zarabljenik," it is translated as "prisoner." From my point of view, it is not a proper translation. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you already went one step beyond what are you expected to do. If you would have said, We should verify that word, that's fine. But to add to that that it is a wrong translation, as it appears here, is one step too far. I will rephrase my question. Mr. Moric, where in the Croatian text of paragraph 3 you see a clear distinction between those civilians and prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what we can see is that they were to be provided uniform treatment in this centre. Equal treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not an answer to my question, because if you are to receive equal treatment, then the question was who would receive equal treatment? And from what I have seen until now, let alone any further translation issues, that the criteria for putting apart some was whether they resided on the territory, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm looking at the clock. We are already far beyond the usual time of having a break. Where I invited you to finish within two sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no further questions. Could I inquire with the other parties how much time they would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I could finish my re-direct within the next session, which would be, let's say, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's well within the next section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions for the Cermak Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that I -- if my learned friend is going take half an hour, I may take approximately that. I have a few documents to clarify. So, say, half an hour, 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which would mean that we could not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think we should be able to finish today, Mr. President. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Well, Mr. Kehoe, you are quite optimistic in the judges having no questions. If we resume at five minutes past 1.00, then two times 30 minutes makes 60 minutes, brings us until five minutes past 2.00. It's complex arithmetics --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I lost of the track of the time, Mr. President, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I lost track of the time, I didn't realise we were so close to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be a common problem, which is more general in this courtroom at this moment. I'm not addressing anyone in particular. We will have a break, and we will resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties who apparently have reached an agreement that it would be preferable to hear Witness Bagic after the recess are invited to make a joint submission, which could, to start with, be an informal submission in an e-mail to be put on the record, If there is any need to do that at a later stage, not only why it is preferable to hear the testimony after the winter recess, but, also, what the compelling reasons are not to hear it before the recess. Because it would result, most likely, in the loss of another couple of days in court. And, of course, this would apply not only to hearing the whole of the evidence before or after the winter recess, but, also, what the compelling reasons are not to hear a part of it, for example, examination-in-chief, before the recess, and the witness be cross-examined after the recess. The Chamber will consider whether it will accept the agreement between the parties in this respect. Mr. Moric, I have another message for you. We will not be able to conclude your testimony today. It will only be tomorrow. I hope that this causes -- that this does not cause you major problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it won't be a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready to further examine Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr Moric.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's resolve a confusion with regard to the terminology and the reception and collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see document P494. This is a document that we have already seen. We saw it during your

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, you had an opportunity to see the entire document. It is dated 4 August. The intention of the document is to say that collection centres should be established in accordance with the intention of the Operation Return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move to the second page of the same document.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: On the seconds page of the document, it is stated that commanders should be appointed and so on and so forth. And it is also stated that security should be provided by the military police, amongst others. Furthermore it says that the conditions in those centres should be in compliance with the Geneva Conventions, and under 1B towards the end of the page it says that the collection centres will accommodate people taken prisoners or detainees, that there will be a register of these people being taken prisoners and that there should be a list of all those who have been brought in. Mr. Moric, as a person's whose mother tongue is Croatian, what, in your view is the term people taken prisoners? How do you define this term?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person taken prisoner is a person who was found in an occupied territory during war activities, and that person either surrendered or was taken prisoner in some other way, which means that it was against that person's will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at another document which was issued one day later, on the 5th August. The number is P1045.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, this document also originates from the Ministry of the Interior. However, the assistant minister who signed the document wasn't you. Let's look at the bottom of the document. We will see that it was Zdravko Zidovec who signed it. He was another assistant minister. Do you remember what his sector was within the Ministry of Interior at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the decree on the internal organisation of the minister of the interior, Mr. Zidovec was in charge of the sector for administrative and logistics tasks, together with the civilian protection and fire-fighters.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: So Mr. Zidovec says in this document, and he also addresses all the police administrations, and says that the police administrations are duty-bound to immediately establish reception centres for civilians. He calls those centres reception centres to distinguish them from collection centres, which were subject from -- of the document from the day before, the 4th of August. And he says: "The centres are to be organised in accordance with the" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is an element of leading in introducing to this question. He calls the centres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic, would you refrain from leading in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do so, Your Honour, although I am not capable to see what was leading in my questions, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, my ruling is that you should put the questions in a non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course. I respect your ruling, Your Honour, as always.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moric we're talking about a document, which deals with the work of reception centres. The document says that the reception centres should be established within -- in compliance with the Geneva Conventions regulating the treatment of civilians. It also says that the reception centres should be established within the organisation of the civilian protection with the full cooperation of regional offices for expelled persons and social work centres. In the second paragraph, it says: "In the course of reception of persons found in the zone of combat activities, i.e., in the liberated area, it is compulsory to separate civilians and send them to the reception centres of the civilian protection." Mr. Moric, if you compare this document with the previous document, what would be your comment? Are we talking about one and the same type of institutions, or are we talking about two different types of institutions?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about two different types of institutions. The previously described centres were for persons who were taken prisoners, and the latter centres for are for civilians, or rather, people who have nothing whatsoever to do with any combat operations or activities.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Let's look at P914. This is a document dated 8 August, three days with respect to the latter document or four days later in respect of the former document, your own, dated the 4th of August. This is a document which was sent on behalf of the Ministry of the Interior of its sector for crime police, was issued by the chief of the sector, Mr. Ivan Nadj on 8th of August. Again, this document was sent to all the police administrations in the area. The subject of the document are collection centres, reference is made to the document dated 4 August that we saw at the beginning of our conversation, Mr. Moric. And the document says: "We are hereby informing you that in the future, instead of the term collection centre for prisoners of war, you are to use the term reception centre for prisoners of war when reporting." Instead of the term reception centre, are you to use the term reception for civilians. Mr. Moric, it is obvious that during the first few days, there were certain awkward uses of the terminology which defined the institutions that received prisoners of war and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Isn't it obvious?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's comment. Okay, Your Honour. I will refrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you will please put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moric, how would you comment the three documents and how would -- what are your thoughts on the terminology and the difference between reception centres, as opposed to the collection centres?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, first if the foundation can be established as to his knowledge of these documents, and secondly the witness has testified on this issue in response to questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Mikulicic is now testing the evidence the witness gave, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but perhaps a foundation could be established as to his knowledge on these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mikulicic was focussing on terminology, not primarily on documents, although this terminology is found in documents, and I therefore consider it to be illustrative rather than anything else at this moment. Could you comment on the terminology, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, obviously in the initial stages, different terms were used to describe reception centres, and they were wrong or unacceptable, and that's why they had to be corrected subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, could you invite the witness to tell us why the terms were wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please answer the Judges question. Why do you think that the terminology was wrong? Maybe a sub-question in this regard. In your order dated 4 August, Mr. Moric, you didn't use the word "civilians." You used the word "prisoners of war." In the order dated 5th of August and signed by Mr. Zidovec, a reference is made to civilians. Doesn't this indicate a difference in the terminology used?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the change or the correction in the use of terminology was caused by the fact that there is a difference in the factual contents. One of the two institutions is a reception centre for war -- prisoners of war, and they are the population who are looked after there, and the other institution is in charge of the victims of war events.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: If the Chamber does not have any question about this topic, I would like to move on to a different subject, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do have a question. Apparently the initial terminology used was collection centre for prisoners of war. That is, the sabirni centar. Now, and apparently, initially, the terminology for the other category was prihvatni centar. If would you not have changed it, would not the distinction between the centres for prisoners of war and the centre for other people, would not -- would that not have been perfectly clear. So the only thing is that you change one word and you change the other word as well; whereas, the difference initially seemed to be rather perfect. The one referring to prisoners of war, and the other one, with a different name, not in any way relating to prisoners of war. So, therefore, the explanation why the initial terminology was wrong is not -- at least I still have difficulties to see why the original terminology did not make a clear distinction. So, therefore I still wonder what then was the reason to replace one clearly distinct terminology between the two categories to be replaced by another, as distinctive terminologies for the -- terminology for the two categories. Is my question clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is clear to me, Your Honour. In my language, the term sabirni, collection, may imply that certain state agencies, in this case the police or the army, was intent on gathering, assembling, collecting people in a given area, and isolating them in the process. The term "prihvatni," reception, in my language, implies that it is a place where individuals are being received who are in need of something or are faced with problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, then, looking at the original language, that you say the sabirni centar for war prisoners was the place where -- sabirni centar is whether you would collect them to get them together, and that should be changed in a place there where -- and I will now literally use your language, that prisoners of war were taken because they were in need of something. I'm following your explanation, your linguistic. You say we changed because we didn't want to collect the war criminals, but we want to bring them to a place where their needs would be fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have expressed myself in a manner that left something to be desired, and you misunderstood me. What I wanted to say was that terminology changed in order to define these facilities in a more precise way, so as to indicate that there was nothing in these facilities that would be contrary to the Geneva Conventions, international conventions, and standards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard your explanation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would like to go back to the decree on the internal structure and the manner of work of the Ministry of Interior which is D527.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call that document up, and more precisely Article 3 of the decree, which is page 2 of the Croatian version and the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We said, Mr. Moric, that the ministry was divided into sectors. We saw that within the special police sector a department was set up, not an office but a department of Internal control. Was there set up a department for internal control in any of the other Ministry of the Interior sectors in addition to the special police sector, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I am not aware of there being a department such as that one in any of the other sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move to Article 8 of the decree now, which defines the work of the internal department -- of the internal control office as part of the minister's office. Article 8.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: I will be focussing on the relevant part of Article 8. Article 8, in fact, provides for the activities of the office for internal control, and let's look at the end of line 3 of the text in Croatian. That the office for internal control shall initiate the work of operative sectors with a view to solving specific cases and shall monitor the proceedings thus initiated until their completion. Of course, this relates to the various types of unlawful conduct on the part of employees. Let's look at Article 8 -- 28 now, which describes the work of the department for internal control of the special police force, of the special police sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 28.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: The department for internal control of the special police shall, it is provided, engage in activities with a view to gathering, processing, and using information concerning the internal order of the special police force, et cetera, et cetera. There is nothing concerning the initiation of the work of the operative sector with a view to resolving specific cases. Mr. Moric, the internal control office attached to the minister's office, did it have jurisdiction over the entire structure of the Ministry of the Interior? That's to say, over all the sectors.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: The competence was to safe-guard the legality, enforce discipline among the employees of the ministry; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: If we look at the tasks envisaged under the decree, the tasks of the internal control department of the special police, we will see that it has to do with providing security to the special police, cooperation with the Service for the Protection of the Constitutional Order, and other security services of the Republic of Croatia. Mr. Moric, the scope of work of the internal control department thus defined, does it indicate that the competence is the same as the one vested with the internal control office attached to the minister's office?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not indicate that the competence is the same, and I can pin-point the difference.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: We will be coming to that point. But, first, can we look at D1092 for -- for illustration. We will see a document issued by the internal control of the special police on the 29th of July, 1995. And the subject is the summary report on the work of reconnaissance-operative groups in the area of Mount Velebit. It is stated here that the internal control department of the special police, on the eve of Operation Storm, engaged in reconnoitring in an area where the special police were supposed to be deployed? Mr. Moric, in your understanding of this document, what is the nature of this report? Is this -- well, I am wary of putting a leading question to you.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on its contents, this is a report, which speaks to the intelligence gathered, the situation in an area which could presumably be the one where the special police would be engaged in operative tasks. In other words, this is intelligence reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D1093 now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: This is a document issued on the 1st of August, 1995, by the office for internal control of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the top of the document, and we will see that it's the 1st of August. We can see that the document was sent to the chief of the staff of the joint forces of the special police. And the document deals with the area of responsibility of the 9th Motorised Brigade, Gracac. The information has to do with the brigade which is deployed as an enemy force opposite the deployment area of the special police. Can you tell us briefly, Mr. Moric, what is the nature of this document.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a word, this is an intelligence report on the situation in an area where the special police may be charged with tasks.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Let us look at D529. What we will be seeing now, Mr. Moric, is a document issued by the internal control on the 11th of January, 1996. It is an annual report of the internal control for the year 1995. This is the internal control of the special police force. The document reads: "In the course of 1995, the office had carried out tasks from within its purview." The report is divided into four parts. The first one being the intelligence and operative preparations of operations in which the special police took part. Part 2 deals with the provision of security for special police units. Part 3, with professional training. And part 4, monitoring the state of work discipline, human relations, relations between special policemen and the command structure, and problems special policemen were faced with. Now, Mr. Moric, part 4, which deals with work discipline, you've already stated repeatedly in your testimony that you were following trends at the level of the ministry. What is your interpretation of item 4, the fact that work discipline was being tackled within special police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It follows clearly from the document that the department dealt with intelligence work, as well as with counter-intelligence, protection of special police units, including monitoring the state of discipline. They go as far as to cover relations among people because that's the sort of thing that was relevant for discipline. Trends in discipline were being monitored, in terms of their improvement or deterioration, in order for them to be able to forestall the negative trends and to support the positive ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the expectation that you would finish in half an hour, I thought that -- but that you would finish within a couple of minutes after quarter to 2.00, but apparently, that is not the case. Therefore, I think it would be better to adjourn. Could you indicate on how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, not more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But I -- with your permission, I will just put one last question. [Overlapping speakers] ... and this is only a matter of a couple of seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question, not more, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question for today, Mr. Moric. Did the office for internal control attached to the office of the minister of the interior deal with such intelligence and counter-intelligence work, as did the internal control department of the special police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Moric, hopefully for the last time I give you the instruction that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, either already given or still to be given tomorrow. I'm not saying to be given the day after tomorrow, because I will not give you the same instructions, most likely, tomorrow. Because we adjourn, and we resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 9th of December, at 9.00, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of December, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.51 p.m.,
